title: Rama's calm
hook: his mother is praying for his coronation when he walks in to tell her

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm. So be it, he said, and honored the vessels meant for him. Today, the hardest conversation: his mother.

Kausalya has been up since before dawn, dressed in white silk by the sacred fire, making offerings for her son's success. She's waited years for this morning. Valmiki tells us she's long been the least favored of the king's wives, and today was going to change that. Then Rama comes in. She's so glad to see him she rises to bless him, and offers him a seat and something to eat. And he has to tell her.
screen: `KAUSALYA AT THE SACRED FIRE.` → `SHE'S WAITED YEARS.` → `AND HE HAS TO TELL HER.`

segments.voice: Rama tells her gently, and she collapses. When she can speak, her grief pours out. If I'd had no son at all, she says, I'd have had one sorrow. Now I have this. She's ready to follow him into the forest. Lakshmana is in the room too, furious; we'll come back to his anger in a few days. Today, watch Rama. He doesn't raise his voice, and he doesn't change his mind. He reminds her of others who obeyed a father's word at great cost, and one example is startling: Parashurama, the sage with the axe we met on the road, who once obeyed his father even against his own mother. Then Rama turns to Kausalya's own path. Your place is with the king, he says. He's old and grieving. Stay with him. Slowly she steadies, and the scene turns. Kausalya stops arguing and starts blessing. She calls on the gods, the seasons, the rivers, the mountains, the days and nights, to protect her son wherever he goes. Valmiki gives her blessing at length, and she ties a protective thread on his arm. Here's the thread back to the Ramayana's first verses, where Valmiki asks Narada: who in the world has mastered himself, ātmavān ko jitakrodho, who has conquered anger? Jitakrodha. Today we see what it looks like. Not a man without feelings, but a son who holds his mother's grief, his brother's rage and his own loss in one room, and stays kind.
screen: `KAUSALYA'S GRIEF POURS OUT.` · `RAMA ANSWERS WITH STEADINESS.` · `HER GRIEF TURNS TO BLESSING.` · `JITAKRODHA: ANGER CONQUERED.` · then, large: `HOLD EVERYTHING, AND STAY KIND.`

segments.voice: Picture someone close to you who's upset right now, about anything; you don't need to fix it. On each breath in, feel a little of what they feel; on each breath out, send them steadiness, the way Rama did for his mother. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Rama's calm, with his mother. He holds Kausalya's grief steadily until her grief turns to blessing: jitakrodha, one who has conquered anger.
Your line: her grief turned to blessing. Tomorrow, the question of blame. That's day five hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Tying a protective thread on someone's wrist before a journey or a rite is still common in Hindu families; in the text, Kausalya blesses Rama at length and ties one on his arm before he leaves.

original.note: Sanskrit jitakrodha: one who has conquered anger, jita (conquered) plus krodha (anger). Valmiki asks after such a person in the epic's first verses.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama is calm because nothing hurts him.
what it means: he stays steady so his mother's grief can turn to blessing.
what a scholar hears: the word jitakrodha in Valmiki's opening question (Bala Kanda 1.4) is a quality the story then shows in scenes like this one.

chat.meaning: Rama held Kausalya's grief steadily and pointed her to her place beside the king, until her grief turned to blessing.

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Confirm the transliteration of Bala Kanda 1.4 (ātmavān ko jitakrodho dyutimān ko 'nasūyakaḥ).
Rama cites Parashurama killing his mother Renuka at Jamadagni's command; the script mentions it only as 'obeyed his father even against his own mother'. Confirm placement (Ayodhya 21).
The protective thread tied by Kausalya: confirm (Ayodhya 25, 'vishalyakarani' herb/amulet in some readings).
Kausalya as the less-favored queen: confirm the text's framing.
